title: The SRA Accounts Rules framework and classifying client money
subtitle: What counts as client money under rule 2.1, and when it stops
objectives: Describe the scope and structure of the SRA Accounts Rules 2019, including why they are shorter and more principles-based than their 1998 predecessor
State the rule 2.1 definition of client money and identify each of its four limbs, including money held on account of costs and unbilled disbursements
Identify the precise point at which money received on account of costs converts from client money into business money

leadingAuthorities.role: Defines 'client money' across its four limbs
Requires client money to be returned promptly once there is no proper reason to retain it
Defines the account in which client money must be held

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Every other lesson in this module assumes you can classify a receipt correctly on sight. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this note appears: 'You know the definition — this lesson is about applying it to money that looks like it should be business money but isn't yet.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on the rule 2.1 wording before. The test pool here leans on fact patterns with figures and dates — expect to work out which limb applies, not recite it.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Slow down through Part 2 and make sure you can list all four limbs of rule 2.1 unprompted before moving on — the rest of the module assumes you can.

overview.hook: A client pays £3,000 'on account of costs' before any work is billed. A week later the solicitor sends a bill for £1,200. Nothing about the money has physically moved, but its legal character has just changed twice. Solicitors Accounts is not about arithmetic — it is about knowing, at any given moment, whose money you are actually holding.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 24 September 2026 under the SRA Accounts Rules 2019 (in force since 25 November 2019). This is a settled, current rulebook; no amendment is pending, though firms should always check the SRA Handbook for the rules currently in force.

parts.heading: Thirteen rules, not four hundred pages
parts.voice: structural — orients the student to the shape of the rulebook before the detail
body: The SRA Accounts Rules 2019 replaced a much longer, more prescriptive 1998 rulebook. Where the old rules ran to dozens of detailed provisions with fixed timeframes, the 2019 version has just 13 rules, built around a small number of outcomes: keep client money safe, keep it separate from the firm's own money, and account for it properly.

This matters for how you should read the rules. They are principles-based rather than mechanical. Instead of a rigid rule saying 'transfer money within 14 days', rule 2.5 simply requires client money to be returned 'promptly' once there is no longer a proper reason to retain it. The judgement is now on the solicitor, not the clock — which means exam questions will test whether you can reason about what 'proper reason' or 'promptly' means on a given set of facts, not whether you can recite a deadline.

The rules apply to all SRA-authorised firms and to the individuals within them who handle client money — not just to a firm's dedicated accounts department. A trainee who receives a cheque at reception is inside the rules from that moment.

components.definition: A regulatory style that states the outcome required (e.g. 'act promptly', 'keep money safe') and leaves the judgement of how to achieve it to the regulated person, rather than prescribing a fixed mechanical rule for every situation.

interaction.prompt: How many rules make up the SRA Accounts Rules 2019?
interaction.modelAnswer: 13 — a deliberately short, principles-based rulebook, replacing the much longer and more prescriptive 1998 Solicitors' Accounts Rules.

parts.heading: Rule 2.1: the four limbs of 'client money'
parts.voice: reference — a checklist part students will return to before every test
body: Everything in this module turns on one question: is a given sum client money or business money? Rule 2.1 answers it. Client money is money a firm holds or receives that falls into any one of four categories.

The first two limbs cover money relating to regulated services — delivered either to the firm's own client, or to a third party (for example, money held as a stakeholder in a transaction where the firm acts for neither side outright). The third limb covers money held in a fiduciary capacity outside an ordinary retainer, such as acting as a trustee, personal representative, or attorney under a power of attorney. The fourth limb is the one that catches students out: money held or received for a firm's own fees and any unpaid disbursements is still client money, for as long as it is held before a bill (or other written notification of costs) has been delivered.

That fourth limb is counter-intuitive on first read — it feels like 'the firm's money' because it will eventually pay the firm's own invoice. But until the bill exists, the client could in principle ask for it back in full, so the rules treat it as client money and require it to sit in the client account.

components.label: The four limbs of rule 2.1 client money
points: Money relating to regulated services delivered by the firm to its own client
Money relating to regulated services delivered to a third party (e.g. stakeholder money)
Money held as trustee, personal representative, attorney, or holder of another specified office or appointment
Money held or received for fees and unpaid disbursements, for as long as no bill or written notification of costs has yet been delivered

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that explains why this £2,000 payment is client money, not business money.
interaction.scenarioText: A new client pays £2,000 into the firm's client account 'on account of costs' before any work has started. No invoice has yet been raised for any of the matter.
tappableSpans: no invoice has yet been raised
interaction.correctSpan: no invoice has yet been raised
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Under the fourth limb of rule 2.1, money held towards fees or disbursements is client money for as long as no bill or written notification of costs has been delivered — the absence of an invoice is what keeps it client money.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The label 'on account of costs' and even the account it sits in aren't what decide its status. What matters is whether a bill has been delivered yet — look again for that fact.

parts.heading: The moment client money becomes business money
parts.voice: worked-example — walks a single scenario through the rule mechanically
body: Suppose a client has paid £3,000 on account of costs, sitting untouched in the client account. The solicitor then delivers a bill for £1,200 of costs incurred to date. What happens to the £3,000 the moment that bill lands?

The £1,200 covered by the bill stops being client money and becomes business money — the firm now has a debt owed to it by the client for that amount, and the corresponding sum in the client account is no longer money 'held on account of unbilled costs'. It must be transferred out of the client account into the business account (this is itself a rule 2.1 mechanic worth remembering: once money stops being client money, it cannot lawfully remain in the client account). The remaining £1,800 stays exactly where it was — still client money, still held on account of costs not yet billed.

This is the trigger to memorise precisely: it is delivery of the bill, or written notification of costs, that converts the money — not the work being done, not the time recorded, and not an internal decision to invoice. Work done but not yet billed leaves money as client money, however confident the firm is that it has earned the fee.

components.text: 'Client money' means money held or received by you relating to regulated services delivered by you to a client, ... including money held or received in respect of your fees and any unpaid disbursements, if held or received prior to delivery of a bill for the same.
elements: Money held or received for fees or unpaid disbursements
Held or received prior to delivery of a bill (or written notification of costs)
Ceases to be client money once that bill or notification is delivered

interaction.prompt: A firm holds £3,000 on account of costs. It delivers a bill for £1,200. What is the status of the money immediately afterwards?
options: The whole £3,000 remains client money until the matter concludes
£1,200 becomes business money and must move to the business account; £1,800 remains client money
The whole £3,000 becomes business money because a bill has now been delivered on the matter
£1,200 becomes business money but may stay in the client account indefinitely
interaction.explanation: Delivery of a bill converts only the billed amount. The unbilled balance is untouched by that bill and remains client money under rule 2.1(d); the billed amount must be transferred out of the client account.

parts.heading: Third-party and fiduciary money: limbs two and three in practice
parts.voice: case-style — grounds the abstract limbs in concrete transactions
body: Limb two is easy to miss because the money is not 'for' the firm's own client at all. A conveyancing firm acting as an escrow agent, holding a deposit that neither buyer nor seller can access until an event occurs, is holding client money for a third party in relation to regulated services — even where that third party has never instructed the firm.

Limb three covers a different situation: a solicitor acting as a professional trustee, personal representative of an estate, or attorney under a lasting power of attorney is not delivering services to a 'client' in the retainer sense at all — the money belongs to a trust, an estate, or a donor. It is still client money for the purposes of the rules, and still must be kept in a client account (subject to the rules' more limited exceptions for certain trustee situations), because the underlying protective purpose is identical: it is not the firm's own money, and the firm must account for it precisely.

The common thread across all four limbs is ownership, not convenience. If the money is not beneficially the firm's own, and it is not yet earned income under a delivered bill, it is client money — regardless of how the file is labelled internally.

components.definition: Money held by a firm on behalf of two or more parties to a transaction pending the occurrence of a specified event (e.g. exchange of contracts), rather than for one client alone — a form of third-party client money under rule 2.1's second limb.

interaction.prompt: A solicitor acts as executor of a deceased client's estate and holds £40,000 of estate funds pending distribution. Is this client money under rule 2.1?
options: Yes — held under the third limb, as money held in the capacity of a specified office such as personal representative
No — an executor is not a client, so the rules on client money do not apply at all
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Limb three of rule 2.1 exists precisely for this situation: fiduciary roles such as executor, trustee or attorney bring the money within the definition even though there is no ordinary client retainer.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at the third limb of rule 2.1 — it is drafted specifically to catch money held in a fiduciary capacity like this, where there is no conventional client relationship at all.

parts.heading: Where classification errors actually bite
parts.voice: argumentative — makes the case for why precision here matters more than it looks
body: It is tempting to treat classification as a formality — 'money is either the client's or the firm's, and everyone roughly knows which'. In practice, misclassifying money at the margins is one of the most common sources of an SRA Accounts Rules breach, because the two errors run in opposite, equally serious directions.

Treating client money as business money too early — spending an unbilled sum, or leaving it in the business account instead of transferring it in — puts client funds at risk and breaches the separation the rules exist to enforce. Treating business money as client money for too long — leaving billed fees sitting in the client account rather than transferring them out promptly — is also a breach, because the client account must not become a parking place for the firm's own income; it undermines the audit trail regulators rely on.

The examiner's fact patterns exploit exactly this symmetry. Expect scenarios where the trap is not 'is this client money at all', but 'has it already stopped being client money' — a bill delivered, a written notification sent, a matter concluded with no proper reason to retain the balance. Read for the triggering event, not just the source of the money.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often assume that because money was originally client money (e.g. paid on account of costs), it stays client money until the matter formally closes.
components.whyItsWrong: Classification changes at the moment a bill or written notification of costs is delivered for that portion of the money — not at the conclusion of the matter. A live matter can have both client money and business money sitting on the same file at once, generated by successive bills.

interaction.prompt: A litigation file has £5,000 held on account of costs. Over the matter, the firm delivers three interim bills of £900 each, none of which have yet been paid out to the business account. What is the correct client-account position right now?
options: All £5,000 must remain in the client account until the matter concludes
£2,700 (the three billed amounts) is business money and should have been transferred out; £2,300 remains client money
Because bills have been delivered, none of the £5,000 is client money any longer
The money became business money the moment the retainer letter was signed
interaction.explanation: Each bill converts only the amount it covers. Three bills of £900 convert £2,700 to business money, which should be transferred out of the client account; the remaining £2,300, never billed, stays client money.

testPool.prompt: A firm receives £500 from a client 'on account of costs' before any bill has been raised. Is this client money or business money?
options: Client money — it falls within rule 2.1(d) until a bill is delivered
Business money — the firm intends to earn fees from it eventually
Neither — money on account of costs is outside the scope of the rules
Business money — because the retainer letter has been signed
testPool.explanation: Money held for unbilled fees or disbursements is client money under rule 2.1(d) for as long as no bill or written notification of costs has been delivered.

testPool.prompt: How many rules make up the SRA Accounts Rules 2019?
testPool.explanation: The 2019 rules are deliberately short — 13 rules built around a small set of outcomes, replacing the far longer and more prescriptive 1998 rules.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the four limbs of the rule 2.1 definition of client money?
options: Money relating to regulated services delivered to the firm's own client
Money held as a trustee or holder of a specified office
Money held for fees and unpaid disbursements before a bill is delivered
Money the firm holds in its own office account for general working capital
testPool.trapExplanation: General working capital in the office (business) account is, by definition, business money — it is the opposite of the four limbs, not a fifth one. Students sometimes list it because it 'sounds like an accounts concept', but it plays no part in the rule 2.1 definition.
testPool.explanation: The four limbs cover money for the firm's own client, money for a third party, fiduciary-capacity money, and unbilled fees/disbursements — not the firm's own working capital.

testPool.prompt: A firm acts as stakeholder holding a £20,000 deposit pending exchange of contracts on a sale, for parties neither of whom the firm formally represents in that role. How should the £20,000 be classified?
options: Business money, because the firm has no client relationship with either party for the stakeholder role
Client money under the second limb of rule 2.1, covering money relating to regulated services delivered to a third party
Client money, but only once exchange of contracts actually occurs
Neither — stakeholder money sits outside the Accounts Rules entirely
testPool.trapExplanation: It is tempting to think 'no client, no client money' — but the second limb of rule 2.1 is drafted specifically to catch money held for a third party in relation to regulated services, which is exactly what stakeholder money is.
testPool.explanation: Stakeholder money is a classic example of the second limb: it is client money even though it is not held for the firm's own client in the ordinary retainer sense.

testPool.prompt: A firm holds £4,000 on account of costs on a probate matter. It delivers a bill for £1,500. The remaining £2,500 is left untouched in the client account. What best describes the position?
options: The whole £4,000 is now business money because a bill has been delivered on the matter
£1,500 is business money and should be transferred to the business account; £2,500 remains client money
£2,500 is business money because it exceeds the billed amount
The client must be asked before any part of the £4,000 changes status
testPool.trapExplanation: Students often let one bill convert the whole balance in their heads. Only the sum actually covered by the bill converts — the rest keeps its original status as unbilled, client money.
testPool.explanation: Delivery of a bill for £1,500 converts only that £1,500. The unbilled £2,500 remains client money under rule 2.1(d) until it too is billed or otherwise returned.

testPool.prompt: A solicitor is appointed as attorney under a lasting power of attorney for an elderly client and holds £15,000 of that client's funds to pay ongoing care costs. How is this money classified under the Accounts Rules?
options: Client money under the third limb, as money held under a specified office or appointment
Business money, because the solicitor is not acting under an ordinary retainer
Outside the Accounts Rules, because attorneyship is a private arrangement
Client money, but only once a bill has been delivered for the attorney work
testPool.explanation: Acting as attorney is exactly the kind of fiduciary office the third limb of rule 2.1 is drafted to capture — money held in that capacity is client money regardless of any retainer.

testPool.prompt: A firm has done £800 of chargeable work on a matter but has not yet sent an invoice or any written notification of costs. Is the £800 currently held as client money?
options: Yes — the money remains client money until a bill or written notification of costs is delivered
No — once the work is done, the money automatically becomes business money
No — because the firm is entitled to be paid for the work
It depends on how long ago the work was completed
testPool.explanation: The trigger is delivery of a bill or written notification of costs, not completion of the underlying work. Until that trigger occurs, the money stays client money, however clearly earned the fee is.

testPool.prompt: A client pays £6,000 on account of costs. The firm sends a letter stating 'please note costs of £2,000 have now been incurred on your matter', without issuing a formal VAT invoice. Does this change the classification of any of the £6,000?
options: No — only a formal VAT invoice can convert client money to business money
Yes — written notification of costs has the same effect as a bill, converting £2,000 to business money
Yes, but only once the client acknowledges receipt of the letter
No — the money only converts when it is physically transferred between accounts
testPool.explanation: Rule 2.1(d) refers to a bill 'or other written notification of costs' — a clear letter stating costs incurred triggers conversion in the same way a formal bill does, even without a VAT invoice.

testPool.prompt: Under rule 2.1(d), what specifically triggers the conversion of money held on account of costs into business money?
options: Delivery of a bill or other written notification of costs for the sum in question
The client's instructions being substantially complete
The passage of 14 days from receipt of the money
The firm recording the time as chargeable in its case management system
testPool.explanation: The rule is precise about the trigger: delivery of a bill or written notification of costs, not the volume of work done, time recorded, or any fixed number of days.

testPool.prompt: Which best describes how the SRA Accounts Rules 2019 differ in style from the 1998 rules they replaced?
options: The 2019 rules are principles-based (e.g. requiring money to be returned 'promptly'), rather than built around fixed mechanical deadlines
The 2019 rules apply only to sole practitioners, not firms
The 2019 rules removed the requirement to keep a client account altogether
The 2019 rules are longer and more detailed than the 1998 rules
testPool.explanation: The defining shift is from prescriptive, mechanical requirements to a shorter, outcomes-focused rulebook that asks for professional judgement, e.g. 'promptly' rather than a fixed day count.

testPool.prompt: Rule 2.5 requires client money to be returned to the client promptly once there is no longer a proper reason to retain it. Which of these is the best example of a 'proper reason' to retain it?
options: The firm intends to use it for a different client's matter temporarily
An undisbursed balance is being held pending an outstanding disbursement that is still expected
The firm has not yet found time to process the return
The client has not asked for it back in writing
testPool.explanation: A genuine, live reason connected to the matter — such as an outstanding disbursement still expected — is a proper reason to retain funds. Administrative delay or client silence are not, and using it for another client's matter is a serious breach in its own right.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following, if true, would bring money within the third limb of rule 2.1 (rather than the first or second limb)?
options: The firm is acting as trustee of a family trust and holds trust funds
The firm holds money on account of costs for its own client
The firm holds a stakeholder deposit for two transacting parties
The firm has delivered a bill for completed work
testPool.explanation: The third limb specifically covers money held in a fiduciary capacity such as trustee, personal representative, or attorney — distinct from money held for a client (first limb) or a third party (second limb).

testPool.prompt: A firm holds £10,000 on account of costs for a corporate client. At the end of the matter, the firm delivers a final bill for £9,200. The client has not responded about the £800 balance six weeks later. What must the firm do?
options: Retain the £800 indefinitely until the client instructs otherwise
Transfer the £800 to the business account, since the matter has concluded
Return the £800 to the client promptly, since there is no proper reason left to retain it
Treat the £800 as an unclaimed balance that can be donated to charity immediately
testPool.trapExplanation: Students sometimes assume silence from the client amounts to permission to keep the money, or that it converts automatically because the matter is over. Neither is right — rule 2.5 requires prompt return once there is no proper reason to retain the money, and silence is not such a reason.
testPool.explanation: Once billed costs are accounted for and no further reason to hold the balance exists, rule 2.5 requires the firm to return the unbilled remainder promptly, regardless of client silence.

testPool.prompt: True or false: a single client matter can have both client money and business money associated with it at the same time.
options: True — successive bills can convert parts of a balance while the rest remains unbilled
False — a matter's funds are always wholly client money or wholly business money
True, but only after the matter has formally concluded
False — the rules require the whole balance to be classified in one go
testPool.explanation: Because conversion happens bill by bill, a live matter routinely has a mix of billed (business) and unbilled (client) money sitting on it simultaneously.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The recurring error in this lesson is assuming client money and business money change status all at once, at some single moment (signing the retainer, finishing the work, or closing the file). In fact conversion happens bill by bill, and only for the amount actually billed — everything else keeps its original character.
